title: Signals and Computed State
summary: Angular's reactive primitives: signal() for state, computed() for derived values, effect() for side effects and linkedSignal() for state that resets, plus how zoneless change detection uses them.
introduction: Signals are how Angular 22 knows what changed. A signal is a box holding a value; reading it records a dependency, writing it notifies everything that depends on it. Templates, computed values and effects all build on that one idea, and it is what lets a zoneless app re-render precisely the parts that need it. This lesson covers the four primitives you will use daily and the mistakes that silently break reactivity.
learningObjectives: Create, read and update signals with signal(), set() and update()
Derive values with computed() and keep dependent state in sync with linkedSignal()
Run side effects with effect() and explain how zoneless change detection relies on signals

blocks.text: Earlier Angular versions used `zone.js` to patch every browser API, run change detection after each event and compare every binding on the page to find out what changed. That worked, but it did a lot of guessing. A signal removes the guesswork: when you call `name.set('Grace')`, Angular knows that exactly the template nodes, computed values and effects which read `name` need attention. Angular 22 projects are zoneless by default, and signals are the mechanism that makes that possible.

`signal(initialValue)` creates a `WritableSignal`. Read it by calling it, replace the value with `set()`, or derive the next value from the current one with `update()`. Signals work in components, services and plain functions alike.

Angular compares the old and new value with `Object.is`, so setting a signal to the value it already holds notifies nobody. For objects and arrays that means a *new* reference is required; mutating the existing one is invisible.

`computed(() => ...)` creates a read-only signal whose value is calculated from other signals. It is **lazy** (not calculated until something reads it) and **memoised** (recalculated only when one of the signals it read has changed). Put every derived value in a `computed()` instead of recalculating it in the template or copying it into a second writable signal.

blocks.title: Common mistake: mutating instead of replacing
blocks.text: `this.prices().push(25)` changes the array but not the signal: the reference is the same, so `count` and `total` are never recalculated and the template does not update. Always produce a new value: `this.prices.update((list) => [...list, 25])`, and for objects `this.user.update((u) => ({ ...u, name: 'Grace' }))`. The same rule applies to `set`.

Templates and computed values are pure: they describe what to show. When a signal change must reach the outside world (write to `localStorage`, set an attribute on `<body>`, log, start a request) use `effect()`. The function runs once when created and again whenever any signal it read has changed. Create effects in the constructor or in a field initialiser, because they need an injection context to register their cleanup.

blocks.text: Effects are batched: three `set()` calls in a row cause one run, not three. If you need to read a signal inside an effect without depending on it, wrap the read in `untracked(() => other())`. And resist the temptation to copy state between signals inside an effect; that is what `computed()` and `linkedSignal()` are for.
linkedSignal(): state that follows other state

Sometimes a value must be editable by the user *and* reset when its source changes: the selected shipping option should be the first available option, until the user picks another, until the options are reloaded. `linkedSignal()` is a writable signal with a computation that recomputes the value whenever its sources change.

blocks.text: Expose signals from services as read-only with `asReadonly()` so that only the service can change them, and keep the writable one private. The [services lesson](/tutorials/angular/services-di) uses exactly that pattern.
How zoneless change detection uses signals

When a template reads a signal, Angular records which view depends on it. Changing the signal marks that view for refresh and schedules a render; nothing else on the page is checked. Template event handlers also mark their component for refresh, which is why a handler that updates a plain property still works. Code that changes state from outside Angular, for instance a callback from a third-party library, should write to a signal or call `ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()`. Keep state in signals and you rarely think about change detection at all.

blocks.title: Signals and RxJS
blocks.text: Observables remain the right tool for streams of events over time, such as web sockets or typed-ahead search. `toSignal()` from `@angular/core/rxjs-interop` turns an observable into a signal for the template, and `toObservable()` goes the other way. The [data lesson](/tutorials/angular/http-resource) shows `toSignal()` with `HttpClient`.

questions.question: Which primitive should hold a `fullName` built from `firstName` and `lastName` signals?
questions.explanation: A derived value belongs in `computed()`: it recalculates only when either name changes and can never drift out of sync.
options: A plain class property set in `ngOnInit`

questions.question: Calling `items().push(x)` on a signal holding an array updates every template that displays the list.
questions.explanation: Pushing mutates the array without changing the signal's reference, so no dependents are notified. Use `items.update((list) => [...list, x])`.
